Expiration actions define when objects\\nare\\nremoved. The effect of these actions depends on the versioning state of your bucket\\nand\\nobjects. Transitions and expirations are asynchronous operations. Your S3 costs, however,\\nare updated as though transitions and expirations were immediate.\\n\\nAmazon S3 has a list of supported lifecycle transitions between storage classes. Additionally, you can\\nchange the default transition behavior so that objects smaller than 128 KB will transition\\nto S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval and S3 Glacier Deep Archive. Upon expiration, Amazon\\n // S3 permanently deletes the noncurrent object versions. You set this lifecycle\\n // configuration action on a bucket that has versioning enabled (or suspended)\\n // to request that Amazon S3 delete noncurrent object versions at a specific\\n // period in the object's lifetime.\\n NoncurrentVersionExpiration *NoncurrentVersionExpiration `type:\\\"structure\\\"`\\n\\n // Specifies the transition rule for the lifecycle rule that describes when\\n // noncurrent objects transition to a specific storage class. If your bucket\\n // is versioning-enabled (or versioning is suspended), you can set this action\\n // to request that Amazon S3 transition noncurrent object versions to a specific\\n // storage class at a set period in the object's lifetime.\\n NoncurrentVersionTransitions []*NoncurrentVersionTransition `locationName:\\\"NoncurrentVersionTransition\\\" type:\\\"list\\\" flattened:\\\"true\\\"`\\n\\n // Prefix identifying one or more objects to which the rule applies. This is\\n // no longer used; use Filter instead.\\n //\\n // Replacement must be made for object keys containing special characters (such\\n // as carriage returns)\\n\\n*[truncated \u2014 additional content omitted]*\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sdk-for-go/api/service/s3/index.html\"},{\"rank_order\":3,\"title\":\"Lifecycle rule details\",\"context\":\"# Lifecycle rule details\\n\\nYou can configure Amazon S3 Lifecycle rules to store your objects cost-effectively\\nthroughout their lifetime. You can instruct Amazon S3 to transition objects to less-expensive\\nstorage classes or to archive or delete objects.\\n\\nUse this page to see the scope of the selected S3 Lifecycle rule. You can also view\\ntransition and expiration actions for current and noncurrent object versions, based\\non your\\nlifecycle rule.\\n\\nFor **Current version actions**, you can see the following\\ninformation:\\n\\n* Since object creation, *the number of days* after\\n which a current version will be transitioned and *the storage\\n class* to transition that version to.\\n* Since object creation, *the number of days* after\\n which a current version will be expired.\\n\\nFor **Noncurrent versions actions**, you can see the following\\ninformation:\\n\\n* Since an object became noncurrent, *the number of\\n days* after which a noncurrent version will be transitioned and\\n *the storage class* to transition that version\\n to.\\n* After the transition, *the number of newest noncurrent\\n versions* to retain.\\n* Since an object became noncurrent, *the number of\\n days* to permanent deletion and *the number of\\n newest noncurrent versions* to retain afterward.\\n\\nUnder **Delete expired object delete markers or incomplete multipart\\nuploads**, there are two sections of configuration information:\\n\\n* You can see if your lifecycle rule is configured to delete expired object delete\\n markers. An expired object delete marker occurs when all object versions are\\n deleted, and only a single delete marker remains. If you selected this option in\\n your lifecycle rule, an expired object delete marker will be deleted.\\n* You can also see if your lifecycle rule deletes incomplete multipart uploads after\\n a specified number of days\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/help-panel/AmazonS3/latest/console/hp-lifecycle-rule-view-page.html\"}]}}"}]}], "label": "Check S3 lifecycle and storage class documentation"}

{"id": "762e2afd-8bea-41b2-abb9-d2b56e8c2590", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"text": "Lifecycle rules cut S3 costs in four ways: they move data to cheaper storage classes, delete data you no longer need, clean up hidden storage, and avoid paying for archive tiers you don't use.

## 1. Transition objects to cheaper storage classes
Add a transition action that moves objects as they age. A typical path looks like this:

| Age | Move to | Good for |
|---|---|---|
| 0 to 30 days | S3 Standard | Hot data |
| 30+ days | Standard-IA or One Zone-IA | Infrequently accessed data that still needs millisecond access |
| 90+ days | Glacier Instant Retrieval | Rarely accessed data that still needs millisecond access |
| 180+ days | Glacier Flexible Retrieval or Deep Archive | Compliance and long-term archives |

If you can't predict access patterns, **S3 Intelligent-Tiering** moves objects automatically. You can use a lifecycle rule to move objects into it.

## 2. Expire data you don't need
- **Expiration** deletes current objects after N days. It suits logs, temp files, and build artifacts.
- **Noncurrent version expiration** deletes old versions in versioned buckets. You can keep the newest N noncurrent versions.
- **Expired object delete markers** are removed so they don't pile up.

## 3. Clean up hidden costs
- **Abort incomplete multipart uploads** after 7 days or so. These leftover parts are billed but don't show up in normal object listings, so many buckets carry them unnoticed.
- In versioned buckets, noncurrent versions are often the biggest source of waste.

## 4. Check the constraints before rolling out
- **Small objects:** by default, S3 won't transition objects smaller than 128 KB. Per-object transition request charges can cost more than the savings on small files. You can override this with an object size filter.
- **Minimum storage durations:** IA and Glacier classes bill a minimum duration (for example, 30 days for Standard-IA). Moving short-lived data there can cost more than leaving it in Standard.
- **Retrieval fees:** IA and Glacier classes charge per GB retrieved. Don't tier data that gets read often.
- **Transition request charges:** every transition costs a per-request fee. This matters for buckets with millions of small objects.
- **Deletes are permanent:** expiration can't be undone. Consider versioning, Object Lock, or replication as a safety net.
- **Scope:** rules can be filtered by prefix, tag, or object size, so you can apply different policies to different data.

## Example rule (JSON)
```json
{
  "Rules": [
    {
      "ID": "logs-tiering",
      "Status": "Enabled",
      "Filter": { "Prefix": "logs/" },
      "Transitions": [
        { "Days": 30, "StorageClass": "STANDARD_IA" },
        { "Days": 90, "StorageClass": "GLACIER" }
      ],
      "Expiration": { "Days": 365 },
      "NoncurrentVersionExpiration": { "NoncurrentDays": 30 },
      "AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload": { "DaysAfterInitiation": 7 }
    }
  ]
}
```

## Where to start
1. Use **S3 Storage Lens** or **Storage Class Analysis** to find the buckets and prefixes with the most cold data, noncurrent versions, and incomplete multipart uploads.
2. Start with the safest wins: abort incomplete multipart uploads and expire noncurrent versions.
3. Then tier cold prefixes by age.
4. Check the cost effect in Cost Explorer after a few weeks.

I can review your actual buckets for you. That means listing each bucket's existing lifecycle rules, versioning status, and size, and flagging the ones with no lifecycle policy. Tell me if you want that, and which account and region to look at.", "type": "text"}], "created_at": null}
